title: The Peak-End Rule

scenes.vo: In one experiment, people chose more pain over less pain. Here's why.

scenes.text: Round 1: hand in ice-cold water for *60 seconds*
scenes.vo: In round one, people kept their hand in ice-cold water for 60 seconds. Ouch.

scenes.text: Round 2: same 60 sec + *30 sec* a bit less cold
scenes.vo: In round two, the same 60 seconds, plus 30 more where the water got a little less cold.

scenes.text:
Which to repeat?
Most chose the *longer* one
scenes.vo: When asked which one they'd do again, most people picked the longer one. More pain, but a nicer ending.

scenes.text: Your brain remembers the *best or worst moment*, and the *ending*
scenes.vo: Your brain doesn't remember how long something lasted. It remembers the most intense moment, and how it ended.
This is called the peak-end rule. Peak means the biggest moment. End means, well, the end.

scenes.text: Great last day of a trip. A bad ending to a movie.
scenes.vo: It's why one great last day makes a whole trip feel amazing, and a bad ending can ruin a whole movie.
So end things well. Presentations, hangouts, even apologies. The ending is what people remember.

caption:
Your memory isn't a video. It's a highlight reel of the biggest moment and the ending. 🎬 That's the peak-end rule.

What movie had an ending that ruined everything? 👇
source: Kahneman, D., Fredrickson, B. L., Schreiber, C. A. & Redelmeier, D. A. (1993). When more pain is preferred to less. Psychological Science, 4(6).
